# SCL for a power-user

> **Reader:** power-user. **Already knows:** the business domain, not the implementation. **Next step:** understand, then confirm the system does the right thing. **Human-constraint budget:** ~7 min read · cognitive load **M**.

The model is the source of truth. This narrative is generated from it.

## Judgements a person owns

Validation cannot certify these. A human owns the judgement.

- `outcome-backwards-compatibility` ⚖ A person decides whether older projects still work, where that is practical.
- `outcome-context-survives` ⚖ A new person can reconstruct the reasons from the project alone.
- `outcome-ai-outcome-aligned` ⚖ A person can tell whether the generated work still serves the outcome.
- `outcome-ai-understanding-inspectable` ⚖ You can read what the assistant assumed before any build starts.
- `outcome-reviewers-understand-min-constraint` ⚖ The write-up is as short as it can be without hiding a risk the reader owns.
- `outcome-uncertainty-visible` ⚖ Open risks stay on a single list, and a recommendation that depends on one says so.
- `outcome-prerequisites-verified` ⚖ Work stops when a critical skill is missing, and says what to restore.
- `outcome-constraints-reliable-not-restrictive` ⚖ Rules block real violations and still allow a new approach that follows the rules.
- `outcome-verification-role-aligned` ⚖ The project checks the right scope and does not keep a second, drifting copy of the truth.

## Releases are consistent and reproducible

Outcomes: `outcome-consistent-frameworks`, `outcome-reproducible-releases`.

The interaction that turns tagged source into a consumable release.

- `requirement-change-docs` (governance, implemented). Every release explains what changed.

## Release quality gates

Outcomes: `outcome-consistent-frameworks`.

The interaction that applies the release quality gates.

- `requirement-validation-instructions` (governance, implemented). Each release tells a consumer how to validate it.
- `requirement-consistency-validation` (governance, implemented). The framework checker reports the tree valid, with zero errors.
- `requirement-refines-discipline-enforced` (governance, implemented). A breakdown stays the same kind of record, stays two levels deep at most, and is not used as a trade-off.

## A release only when consumers are affected

Outcomes: `outcome-predictable-upgrades`, `outcome-releases-mean-consumer-impact`.

The interaction that decides whether a change set is allowed to become a release.

- `requirement-release-eligibility` (governance, implemented). A release is cut only when a project-consumable asset changed. Internal-only edits are recorded as framework work, not a release.
- `requirement-consumer-impact-test` (governance, implemented). Before a release, answer whether a project on the previous release would behave differently. If yes, record the difference.

## Four-step release lifecycle

Outcomes: `outcome-releases-mean-consumer-impact`, `outcome-predictable-upgrades`.

The interaction that moves a meta-model from candidate to a human green light.

- `requirement-lifecycle-four-steps` (governance, implemented). A release candidate is generated from the model, tested, and shipped only on a documented human green light.
- `requirement-model-is-source-of-truth` (governance, implemented). Generated documents are derived from the model. When they disagree, the model wins and the document is regenerated.

## AI tools can consume the assets

Outcomes: `outcome-ai-consumable`.

The interaction in which a tool reads a project manifest and resolves version, model location, and upgrade eligibility.

- `requirement-version-discovery` (functional, implemented). A tool can read the project file and learn the framework version, where the model lives, and whether an upgrade applies.

## The model captures why

Outcomes: `outcome-intent-visible`, `outcome-context-survives` ⚖, `outcome-ai-outcome-aligned` ⚖.

The interaction in which an author records why the work exists, in the repository, and refuses to invent a missing interaction.

- `requirement-capture-why` (governance, implemented). The model records why the work exists, not only the rules, and every rule traces back to that why.
- `requirement-context-persistent-inspectable` (non-functional, implemented). A new person can reconstruct the reasons from the project alone, without asking someone who has left.
- `requirement-raise-gap-challenge` (governance, implemented). A suspected missing interaction becomes a challenge with an observation, a concern, possibilities, and a question. It is not added as a fact.
- `requirement-model-holds-test-preconditions` (governance, planned). Preconditions, the trigger, and the expected result live in the model before any test is written.

## Human-authored mode

Outcomes: `outcome-ai-outcome-aligned` ⚖.

The interaction in which a person authors the chain and the assistant treats requirements as hard boundaries.

- `requirement-support-human-authored-mode` (functional, implemented). A person writes the chain. The assistant does not invent records, and requirements stay hard boundaries.

## AI understanding is inspectable before implementation

Outcomes: `outcome-ai-outcome-aligned` ⚖, `outcome-ai-understanding-inspectable` ⚖.

The interaction in which the assistant proposes a slice and waits for a person to approve it.

- `requirement-support-ai-inferred-mode` (functional, implemented). The assistant may propose a slice from a high-level request. The slice is marked proposed and inferred, and nothing is built until a person approves it.
- `requirement-expose-ai-understanding` (governance, implemented). Every inferred record states what was inferred, so a person can catch a wrong assumption before implementation.
- `requirement-emergent-design-surfaced` (governance, planned). A design choice no requirement dictated, which would shape what a person sees, becomes a proposed decision. Incidental choices stay free.

## The reviewer understands the system at minimum cost

Outcomes: `outcome-reviewers-understand-min-constraint` ⚖.

The interaction that generates one narrative per reader role from the model.

- `requirement-narrative-per-role` (functional, implemented). There is a separate narrative for a developer, a tester, and a power user. Each names the role, what that reader knows, and the next step.
- `requirement-narrative-role-scope` (functional, implemented). A developer and a tester see every requirement. A power user sees the business-facing ones, and a technical requirement only as the consequence they own.
- `requirement-narrative-human-constraint-budget` (non-functional, implemented). The write-up tells you how long it takes to read and does not hide a risk to stay short.
- `requirement-narrative-traceable` (governance, implemented). Regenerating from the model reproduces the narrative, and every requirement the developer narrative names exists in the model.
- `requirement-narrative-flag-manual-eval` (governance, implemented). Where a person rather than a machine must judge, the narrative shows the judgement marker.

## Unresolved uncertainty stays visible

Outcomes: `outcome-uncertainty-visible` ⚖.

The interaction that keeps one list of unresolved questions and makes recommendations name the ones they depend on.

- `requirement-open-questions-central` (governance, implemented). meta/open-questions.md is the only independent list. Anything else refers to a question by id.
- `requirement-open-question-fields` (governance, implemented). Each question has eleven fields, and the risk level is one of Critical, High, Medium, Low, or Informational.
- `requirement-open-question-influence` (governance, implemented). A recommendation that depends on an unresolved High or Critical question names it, names the risk, and says results may change once it is resolved.

## Required skills are verified first

Outcomes: `outcome-prerequisites-verified` ⚖.

The interaction that discovers skills, verifies them, and only then runs a significant operation.

- `requirement-skills-registry` (governance, implemented). meta/required-skills.md lists each skill with five fields: id, name, purpose, criticality, and verification.
- `requirement-verify-skills-before-ops` (governance, implemented). The harness discovers skills, verifies them, and only then runs the operation. A missing critical skill stops the run and names the skill, the impact, and the action.

## Constraints bound solutions without restricting them

Outcomes: `outcome-constraints-reliable-not-restrictive` ⚖.

The interaction that executes within layer roles and fails a solution only on a real boundary violation.

- `requirement-interpreter-honours-layers` (functional, implemented). Intent dominates, outcomes are what you optimise, models are the logical shape, and requirements are hard boundaries. The engine's private method is not prescribed.
- `requirement-no-expressiveness-penalty` (governance, implemented). Only a real boundary violation may fail a solution. Failing a new approach that still follows the rules is a defect.

## Verification role

Outcomes: `outcome-verification-role-aligned` ⚖.

The interaction that will adopt a development or solution-test role from the project manifest. Not built yet.

- `requirement-unit-scope-single-model` (functional, planned). In development, a check covers only the requirements that constrain the one model an artefact realises.
- `requirement-solution-scope-trace-chain` (functional, planned). In solution testing, a check walks the model up to the intent, against a read-only pinned snapshot.
- `requirement-repin-triage` (governance, planned). Moving the pinned model forward marks each affected chain unchanged, deliberately changed, or broken. A broken chain stops the move. A deliberate change must be confirmed first.
- `requirement-solution-coverage` (governance, planned). Every in-scope outcome has at least one test, and every machine-checkable requirement has at least one test. Gaps are named as model elements, not as lines of code.
